hints: Count carbons carefully, 1-bromobutane has four carbons and the cyanide ion adds one extra carbon to the chain.
walkthrough:
Spot the chain extension**
Think of what $\text{CN}^{-}$ does. It swaps for $\text{Br}$ but it brings its own carbon with it. So you start with a 4 carbon bromoalkane and you finish with a 5 carbon nitrile. That is why P must be $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CN}$.

Draw displayed correctly**
Displayed means show every atom and every bond. Write $\text{N}\equiv\text{C}$ with a triple bond, then single bonds to each $\text{CH}_{2}$ group, ending in $\text{CH}_{3}$. Show all H atoms on each carbon.
Final answer: Fully displayed $\text{N}\equiv\text{C-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{3}$ with all C-H and C-C bonds shown, pentanenitrile.

hints: Look at what P changes into, a nitrile turning into $\text{CH}_{3}(\text{CH}_{2})_{3}\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ is hydrolysis, what type of reagent hydrolyses nitriles?
Compare reaction 2 forming but-1-ene with the $\text{OH}^{-}(aq)$ route forming an alcohol, what solvent favours elimination over substitution?
walkthrough:
Identify reaction 1 as hydrolysis**
P is a nitrile, $\text{R-CN}$, and the product is a carboxylic acid, $\text{R-CO}_{2}\text{H}$. That is acid hydrolysis. You need dilute aqueous acid, typically $\text{HCl}(aq)$, heated under reflux to supply water and $\text{H}^{+}$ catalyst.

Identify reaction 2 as elimination**
1-bromobutane to but-1-ene removes $\text{HBr}$. That is dehydrohalogenation. Aqueous $\text{OH}^{-}$ would give substitution to an alcohol, so for elimination you need concentrated $\text{NaOH}$ or $\text{KOH}$ in ethanol, heated. Ethanol as solvent favours elimination.

Final answer: reaction 1: dilute $\text{HCl}(aq)$, heat under reflux
reaction 2: conc. $\text{NaOH}$ / $\text{KOH}$ in ethanol, heat

hints: Recall that addition polymerisation opens the C=C double bond to give a saturated C-C backbone with two new single bonds to neighbours.
Draw but-1-ene as $\text{CH}_{2}=\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ and think which two groups stay attached to the two backbone carbons.
walkthrough:
Open the double bond**
Write but-1-ene out: $\text{CH}_{2}=\text{CH-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{3}$. In addition polymerisation the pi bond breaks and each of the two C atoms forms a new sigma bond to the next monomer. So the backbone becomes single $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-CH-}$ units linked together.

Keep the side chain**
The ethyl group $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ never reacts, it just hangs off the second carbon. So your repeat unit has $\text{CH}_{2}$ then $\text{CH}(\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5})$, with a dangling bond on each side to show continuation of the chain. Do not show the double bond and do not add extra H atoms.

Final answer: Repeat unit: $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}(\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5})\text{-}$ shown with continuation bonds through the backbone carbons, i.e. $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}(\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3})\text{-}$

hints: Decide the roles, $\text{OH}^{-}$ is the nucleophile with a lone pair and the $\delta+$ carbon attached to Br is the electrophile.
Remember the two curly arrows in one concerted step, one to form the new C-O bond and one to break the C-Br bond.
Think what organic product forms when $\text{Br}$ in 1-bromobutane is replaced by $\text{OH}$.
walkthrough:
Set up nucleophile and electrophile**
$\text{OH}^{-}$ has full negative charge and lone pairs, it loves positive centres. In $\text{C-Br}$, Br is more electronegative than C, so show $\text{C}^{\delta+}\text{-Br}^{\delta-}$. That $\delta+$ carbon is your target.

Draw the attack arrow**
Start a curly arrow on a lone pair on O and point it to the $\delta+$ carbon. This shows the new $\text{C-O}$ bond forming. At the same time start a second curly arrow in the middle of the $\text{C-Br}$ bond and point it to Br, showing $\text{Br}^{-}$ leaving. For a primary haloalkane this is concerted.

Finish with the product**
The $\text{OH}$ is now covalently attached to the chain, giving $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$, which is R, butan-1-ol, plus $\text{Br}^{-}$. Check you have charges, dipoles, lone pair and both arrows.

Final answer: Lone pair on $\text{O}$ of $\text{OH}^{-}$ attacks $\delta+$ C of C-Br, curly arrow $\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}$; $\text{C}^{\delta+}\text{-Br}^{\delta-}$ dipole shown, curly arrow $\text{C-Br} \rightarrow \text{Br}$ to form $\text{Br}^{-}$; product $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$, butan-1-ol.

hints: Focus on the C=C bond in but-1-ene and steam adding H and OH across it, what general class of alkene reaction is this?
walkthrough:
Recognise addition across C=C**
But-1-ene $\text{CH}_{2}=\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ plus steam $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ gives a single alcohol product with H added to one carbon and OH to the other. Two reactants become one product with no loss, that is the signature of addition. Because the alkene pi bond attacks an electrophile first, it is electrophilic addition.
Final answer: (electrophilic) addition

hints: Recall which structural feature gives a yellow precipitate with alkaline aqueous iodine, both methyl ketones and the related secondary alcohol do this.
walkthrough:
Link positive iodine test to structure**
Alkaline aqueous iodine is the iodoform test. A yellow precipitate of $\text{CHI}_{3}$ means you have $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO-}$ or $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)-}$ which can be oxidised in situ to $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO-}$. Since S is an alcohol, it must contain $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)-}$.
Final answer: S contains $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)-}$ group, a methyl group adjacent to a CHOH group.

hints: Picture proton addition to but-1-ene giving two possible carbocations, a primary one on C1 and a secondary one on C2.
Think how alkyl groups push electron density toward a positive carbon and which intermediate this stabilises more.
walkthrough:
Compare the two possible intermediates**
Adding $\text{H}^{+}$ to $\text{CH}_{2}=\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ can give $\text{CH}_{3}\text{-CH}^{+}\text{-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ (secondary) or $^{+}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ (primary). The secondary route leads to S, butan-2-ol, the primary route leads to T, butan-1-ol.

Explain stability with inductive effect**
Alkyl groups donate electron density by the positive inductive effect, spreading and reducing the positive charge. The secondary carbocation has two alkyl groups attached to $\text{C}^{+}$ versus only one for the primary, so it is more stable, lower in energy, forms faster, and gives the major product. This is Markovnikov addition.

Final answer: Alkyl groups have a positive inductive effect, donating electron density to the carbocation centre.
The secondary carbocation leading to S is more stable than the primary carbocation leading to T, so S forms preferentially.

hints: Use the major versus minor labels plus the iodoform result to decide which alcohol is butan-2-ol and which is butan-1-ol.
Remember that reflux with $\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}^{2-}$/$\text{H}^{+}$ oxidises a secondary alcohol to a ketone with the same skeleton.
Recall skeletal rules, each corner and end is a carbon with enough H to make four bonds, and C=O is shown explicitly.
walkthrough:
Assign S and T**
Hydration of but-1-ene gives two structural isomers. The major product S must be the Markovnikov product with OH on C2, so $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, butan-2-ol. This also fits the iodoform test. The minor product T is anti-Markovnikov with OH on C1, so $\text{HOCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, butan-1-ol.

Assign U by oxidation**
S is a secondary alcohol, so strong oxidation under reflux with acidified dichromate gives a ketone, not an aldehyde or acid. Simply change CH(OH) to C=O with the same carbon skeleton: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, butan-2-one. U also gives a positive iodoform test, consistent with a methyl ketone.

Draw skeletal correctly**
In skeletal formulae, draw zigzags. S is a four carbon zigzag with OH on the second carbon. T is a four carbon zigzag with OH on the end carbon. U is a four carbon zigzag with a double bond O on the second carbon. Do not write CH3 or CH2 labels, just lines, except for OH and O.

Final answer: S = $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, butan-2-ol
T = $\text{HOCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, butan-1-ol
U = $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, butan-2-one, all as skeletal formulae.

hints: Write S plus [O] going to U plus water and balance H and O, the carbon skeleton does not change.
walkthrough:
Balance with [O]**
Put down S as $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ and U as $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$. You remove two H atoms overall, one from O and one from C, so you need one [O] to combine with them to make $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. Check atoms: one O on each side plus water balances, so the equation is $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3} + [\text{O}] \rightarrow \text{CH}_{3}\text{COCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$.

hints: Name the ester from the alcohol part first then the acid part, methanol plus pentanoic acid gives which alkyl alkanoate?
walkthrough:
Name the ester**
Carboxylic acid plus alcohol with acid catalyst gives ester plus water: $\text{CH}_{3}(\text{CH}_{2})_{3}\text{CO}_{2}\text{H} + \text{CH}_{3}\text{OH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_{3}(\text{CH}_{2})_{3}\text{CO}_{2}\text{CH}_{3} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. The alkyl from the alcohol comes first, methyl, then the acid part as alkanoate, pentanoate. So V is methyl pentanoate.

hints: List the key functional groups in the three compounds, pentanoic acid has C=O and O-H, methanol has O-H only, the ester V has C=O only.
Recall where C=O absorbs, a sharp strong peak near $1730 \text{ cm}^{-1}$, which spectra show this?
Recall where O-H absorbs, a broad peak above $2500 \text{ cm}^{-1}$, which spectra show this?
Combine the two observations to find the spectrum with C=O but no O-H.
walkthrough:
List what each compound should show**
$\text{CH}_{3}(\text{CH}_{2})_{3}\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ has both $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{O-H}$ (carboxylic acid). Methanol $\text{CH}_{3}\text{OH}$ has $\text{O-H}$ but no $\text{C=O}$. Ester V, $\text{CH}_{3}(\text{CH}_{2})_{3}\text{CO}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, has $\text{C=O}$ but no $\text{O-H}$. That contrast is the key.

Find the C=O peak**
Look above $1500 \text{ cm}^{-1}$. X and Z both have a strong sharp absorption at about $1730 \text{ cm}^{-1}$, characteristic of $\text{C=O}$ stretch. Y has no peak there, so Y must be methanol.

Find the O-H absorption**
Y shows a very broad band centred near $3300 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ for alcohol O-H. Z shows a very broad band from about $2500$ to $3300 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ for carboxylic acid O-H. X has no broad absorption above $2500 \text{ cm}^{-1}$, only sharp C-H stretches near $2900 \text{ cm}^{-1}$.

Match V**
V needs $\text{C=O}$ present and O-H absent. Only X fits both criteria, so V is X. By elimination, Z is the carboxylic acid and Y is methanol.

Final answer: V is spectrum X.
Spectra X and Z show $\text{C=O}$ stretch at $1730 \text{ cm}^{-1}$.
Spectra Y and Z show O-H stretch above $2500 \text{ cm}^{-1}$.
V is an ester with $\text{C=O}$ and no O-H, so only X fits.
